PAPER: Mind the Jumps: A Scalable Robust Local Gaussian Process for Multidimensional Response Surfaces with Discontinuities Isaac Adjetey∗ and Yiyuan She† Abstract Modeling response surfaces with abrupt jumps and discontinuities remains a major challenge across scientific and engineering domains. Although Gaussian process models excel at capturing smooth non- linear relationships, their stationarity assumptions limit their ability to adapt to sudden input-output variations. Existing nonstationary extensions, particularly those based on domain partitioning, often strugglewithboundaryinconsistencies,sensitivitytooutliers,andscalabilityissuesinhigher-dimensional settings, leading to reduced predictive accuracy and unreliable parameter estimation. To address the challenges posed by data heterogeneities and high dimensions, this paper proposes theRobustLocalGaussianProcess(RLGP)model,anovelframeworkthatintegratesadaptivenearest- neighbor selection with a sparsity-driven robustification mechanism. Unlike existing methods, RLGP leveragesanoptimization-basedmean-shiftrobustificationafteramultivariateperspectivetransformation combinedwithlocalneighborhoodmodelingtomitigatetheinfluenceofoutliers. Thisapproachenhances predictive accuracy near discontinuities while improving resistance to data heterogeneity. Comprehensive evaluations on real-world datasets show that RLGP consistently delivers high pre- dictive accuracy and maintains competitive computational efficiency, especially in scenarios with sharp transitions and complex response structures. Scalability tests further confirm RLGP’s stability and re- liability in higher-dimensional settings, where other methods falter. These outcomes establish RLGP as an effective and practical solution for modeling nonstationary and discontinuous response surfaces, applicable across a wide range of real-world scenarios. Standard Gaussian Process (GP) models are highly valued for their flexibility in capturing nonlinear relationships and for providing statistical predictions and estimates, enabling partially analytic inference (Paciorek and Schervish, 2006; Heinonen et al., 2016). In particular, the ability to quantify prediction un- certainty makes them particularly useful in applications where knowing how reliable a prediction is matters as much as the prediction itself (Wang and Haaland, 2019; Neto and Schmidt, 2020). However, the sta- tionarity assumption inherent in conventional GP models restricts their ability to adapt to environments with abrupt shifts in input-output dynamics (Gramacy and Lee, 2008). Moreover, inaccurate predictions and unreliable uncertainty estimates jeopardize downstream tasks, including failure region identification (Wang et al., 2016), sequential experimental design (McKay et al., 2000), simulator calibration (Kennedy and O’Hagan, 2001), and sensitivity analysis (Rohmer and Foerster, 2011). Addressing nonstationary yet realistic response patterns remains a fundamental challenge in surrogate modeling (Heaton and Peng, 2012; Pandita et al., 2021). Efforts to address localized complexities lead to the development of nonstationary GP methods, which can be categorized as follows. 1. Kernel-based spatial modeling. Higdonetal.(1999),PaciorekandSchervish(2003),andKatzfuss (2013) introduce spatially varying covariance structures to model abrupt transitions in the response surface. However, these approaches still display residual correlation for observations near regional boundaries may. 2. Partition models. Kim et al. (2005) and Pope et al. (2021) employ Voronoi tessellation to divide the input space into triangular regions, while Luo et al. (2021) uses Delaunay triangulation to con- struct spatial adjacency graphs. Within each region, an independent stationary GP is fitted, and both the number of partitions and model parameters are inferred jointly using Bayesian sampling. The tessellation-based approaches perform well when d = 2, but their computational complexity increases significantlywithdimensionality,limitingtheirscalabilityandapplicabilitytohigher-dimensionalprob- lems. However, as dimensionality increases, their recursive partitioning along coordinate axes leads to combinatorial complexity, making them computationally prohibitive. Additionally, poor partitioning can either excessively fragment the space, leaving too little data in each region, or fail to sufficiently dividethespace,missingabruptresponsejumps. Park (2022) highlight their limitations in handling real-world variations across complex regional boundaries. 3. Neighborhood-based models. Emergingmethodologicaladvancesleveragea“transductive”frame- work(SchwaighoferandTresp,2002),wherethetestdataitselfguidesthetrainingprocess,dynamically refining training data selection to enhance predictive accuracy at individual test locations. One of the earlier approaches, the local approximate GP (Gramacy and Apley, 2015), improves computational efficiency by constructing a GP model using only the nearest neighbors of the test point, thereby reducing complexity while maintaining accuracy. More recently, the locally induced GP (Cole et al., 2021) extends this idea by selecting induced points based on local structure rather than relying solely 2 on proximity, offering a more flexible and adaptive representation. Building on these concepts, more recently, the jump GP (Park, 2022) further refined local data selection by first identifying relevant neighbors and then segmenting them using a parametric hyperplane or partitioning function. This partitioning function can be linear, quadratic, or even cubic, depending on the complexity of the local data, ensuring that a GP is fitted specifically to the subset containing the test location. Generally speaking, these neighborhood-based methods perform well when the test point is deep within a ho- mogeneous region, but face difficulties near region boundaries, where conflicting trends from adjacent areas degrade prediction accuracy (cf. Figure 1). This boundary issue becomes more severe in high dimensions, further reducing accuracy and complicating robust inference. 4. Probabilistic deep models. A distinct category of methods learns global, hierarchical representa- tionsofthedatatoimplicitlymodelnon-stationarity. BayesianNeuralNetworks(BNNs)(Jospinetal., 2022), for example, place distributions over network weights to capture parameter uncertainty, allow- ing the model to adapt to complex functions. Deep Gaussian Processes (DeepGPs) (Damianou and Lawrence, 2013) compose multiple GP layers, creating a deep architecture that learns a flexible, non- linear warping of the input space. While these models are highly expressive and can capture intricate data patterns without explicit partitioning, that power comes at the cost of increased computational complexity, which in turn can affect accuracy as it often requires approximate inference techniques to ensure scalability. Consequently, a feasible yet unexplored approach is to systematically identify and downweight the in- fluence of extraneous data within a local neighborhood, particularly when dealing with conflicting data patterns from adjacent regions that exhibit distinct response dynamics. Indeed, most approaches fail to iso- late the most relevant local trends (Waelder et al., 2024), undermining both interpretability and predictive reliability. Furthermore, their application is often limited to dimensions (e.g., ≤ 10 dimensions) far below application needs. JSON: Name: robust_local_gp Title: Robust local Gaussian process with multivariate perspective transformation and sparse mean-shift regularization for modeling discontinuous multidimensional response surfaces Short Hypothesis: Integrating a multivariate perspective transformation and a sparse mean-shift outlyingness parameter into an adaptive nearest-neighbor local Gaussian process reduces point-prediction mean squared error and improves predictive distribution calibration near input-space discontinuities compared to standard local Gaussian process and partitioning-based methods. Related Work: Existing approaches for modeling nonstationary or discontinuous response surfaces fall into four broad classes: (1) spatially varying kernel methods that modify covariance structure to allow local nonstationarity; (2) partition-based methods that divide the input space (e.g., tessellations or tree recursion) and fit independent GPs per partition; (3) neighborhood/transductive local GP variants that construct per-query local training sets; and (4) probabilistic deep models (Bayesian neural nets, deep GPs) that learn hierarchical nonstationary mappings. Limitations shared across these approaches include: spatial-kernel methods retain residual boundary correlation and can misrepresent abrupt jumps; partition methods suffer boundary inconsistencies, sensitivity to partitioning strategy, combinatorial complexity and poor scalability in high dimensions; existing neighborhood methods degrade near region boundaries due to contaminating neighbors and lack explicit robustification; deep probabilistic models require heavy approximate inference, are sensitive to architectural choices, and can be computationally expensive and memory intensive. Robust, scalable strategies that explicitly detect and downweight local contaminating observations while remaining efficient in high dimensions remain unresolved. Abstract: Modeling multidimensional response surfaces that contain abrupt jumps and local heterogeneity challenges standard Gaussian process (GP) surrogates because stationarity and global smoothness assumptions blur discontinuities and yield unreliable uncertainty estimates. We propose a robust local GP framework that (i) constructs adaptive nearest-neighbor subdesigns around each query, (ii) applies a multivariate perspective transformation to stabilize covariance/scale estimation, and (iii) introduces a sparse mean-shift parameter to identify and remove contaminating local observations via l0-type regularization. Parameter estimation is performed with a scalable block-coordinate optimization that uses iterative quantile thresholding for sparse outlier selection and quasi-Newton updates for covariance hyperparameters. The primary contribution is an integrated, optimization-driven local GP that explicitly detects and neutralizes boundary-contaminating observations while retaining principled predictive distributions. We expect the method to yield lower prediction error and better-calibrated predictive uncertainty near discontinuities, with computational cost suitable for problems with hundreds of input dimensions. The approach targets applications where local discontinuities and heterogeneous noise degrade standard surrogate models. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Nanotube: n=52 experimental runs; evaluate with leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV). (2) CSImage: 17,519 adaptively sampled spatial points; random 90/10 train/test split. (3) Corrosion: 10,153 sensor readings; random 90/10 split. (4) Cancer (CCLE RPPA subset): 899 cell lines; 90/10 split. (5) Synthetic high-dimensional partitioned GP: dimensions d ∈ {10,25,50,75,100,150,200,250,300,350,400,500}; training n=10d via Latin hypercube sampling; test set size 1000; repeat each configuration 20 independent random seeds. Baselines: Treed GP (TGP), Dynamic Trees, local GP, laGP, liGP, Jump GP (linear and quadratic partitions), Deep GP, Bayesian Neural Network (BNN). Metrics: point-prediction MSE, predictive CRPS, negative log predictive density (NLPD), 95% interval empirical coverage, average runtime per test point, peak RAM, and outlier detection precision/recall (where ground truth known in synthetic). Experimental setup: default RLGP uses adaptive q determined by Tukey MAD rule; neighborhood sizes n ∈ {50,100,200,500} evaluated; covariance kernels compared: squared-exponential and Matern (ν=3/2); optimization uses block-coordinate descent with iterative quantile thresholding for γ, quasi-Newton for hyperparameters; perform 20 repeated trials per dataset/configuration with different random seeds; report mean and standard error across repeats. Ablation studies: (A) adaptive-q vs fixed q ∈ {0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30}; (B) remove perspective transformation (standard Σ parametrization); (C) replace l0 quantile thresholding with l1 penalty solved by proximal gradient; (D) disable mean-shift (γ=0) to emulate standard local GP; (E) optimization comparison: BCD (proposed) vs joint quasi-Newton on all parameters. Statistical tests: paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on MSE and CRPS across repeats between RLGP and each baseline; significance threshold α=0.05 with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. Implementation notes: measure wall-clock time and peak memory on a fixed CPU node (single core) and report per-test statistics aggregated over all test points. Risk Factors and Limitations: Optimization and convergence: the nonconvex l0-constrained problem and block-coordinate scheme may converge to local optima; quantile-thresholding may produce different supports for γ across runs. Modeling assumptions: the mean-shift parameterization assumes sparsely located gross outliers; failure modes arise when contamination is dense or when heterogeneity is smoothly varying (not well represented by sparse shifts). Neighborhood selection: nearest-neighbor subdesigns degrade in very high ambient dimensions due to distance concentration (curse of dimensionality), reducing effective locality. Kernel dependence: performance depends on the choice of covariance kernel and its length-scale scaling in high dimensions; mis-specified kernels can yield poor predictive variance estimates. Scalability limits: per-query local matrix factorizations scale cubically with neighborhood size n; very large n or extreme test-set sizes increase runtime and memory. Uncertainty calibration: plug-in hyperparameter estimates may understate epistemic uncertainty relative to full Bayesian inference. Data biases and evaluation: real datasets may contain unobserved confounders or correlated noise patterns that invalidate the sparse outlier model; evaluation based on synthetic partitions may not encompass all types of real discontinuities. Reproducibility: results can be sensitive to implementation choices (numerical tolerances, initialization) and to the chosen adaptive q heuristic.
